dish: mantu (beef dumplings in tomato-yogurt), kabuli palaw, sautéed pumpkin (kadu), chapli & chicken kabobs
w: The dressiest and most enduring Afghan house in the Bailey's Crossroads corridor (since 2005), where Washingtonian's Cheap Eats singled out the mantu, caramelized eggplant and sweet-tart pumpkin, and the Washington Post's 'Y Not Try Bamian?' called it 'the dressiest place in the area to sample bulanee and mantu.' Tyler Cowen's Ethnic Dining Guide rates it 'one of the best Afghan places around,' praising juicy kabobs. Open and busy into 2026.

dish: sundubu jjigae (soft-tofu soup), seafood pancake, banchan
w: The Annandale Koreatown soft-tofu specialist (a.k.a. Vit Goel Tofu) whose bubbling sundubu jjigae earned a fresh January 2026 Washington Post review — 'remains as good as ever' — under hanok-style papered windows. Northern Virginia Magazine's 'Meaty Monday' column had already praised it. A comforting counterpoint to the corridor's grill houses; consistently high volume across platforms.

dish: dry-aged Korean BBQ (prime brisket, wagyu), original steakhouse creations
w: The upscale Korean steakhouse that the Honest Grill team (chef Danny Kim, ex-Clarity) opened in downtown Falls Church in late 2024, kicking Korean BBQ into fine-dining territory. Washingtonian ('Seoul Prime Brings Upscale Korean Barbecue to Falls Church'), Northern Virginia Magazine and Arlington Magazine all ran features within months of opening — one of the corridor's most-talked-about new Korean rooms.

dish: kitfo (raw ground beef with mitmita), yellow lentils, shiro, gomen
w: A Bailey's Crossroads kitfo house whose specialty Tyler Cowen's Ethnic Dining Guide calls flatly 'the best kitfo around, period,' adding it also has 'the best yellow lentils around.' Annandale Today covered its opening. A focused, community-facing addition to the region's dense East African corridor, where Meaza anchors the tier-1 slot.

dish: kare-kare, dinuguan, lechon kawali, pancit, lumpia, halo-halo
address: 2946 Sleepy Hollow Rd, Falls Church, VA 22044
w: A cozy Falls Church diner that owner Solita turned into one of the few full Filipino kitchens inside the Beltway, cooking classics from her home province of Pampanga (the Philippines' culinary capital). Asian Fortune profiled it as 'A Rare Filipino Gem Within the Beltway' and Visit Fairfax lists it among Fairfax County's Filipino tables; still open and reviewed into 2026.

dish: Sichuan chili chicken (on the bone), braised fish, cumin lamb
w: The Fairfax strip-mall Sichuan destination where cult chef Peter Chang first cooked in the DC area — the restaurant at the center of Calvin Trillin's New Yorker 'Where's Chang?' saga. It has stayed superb under his successors, who kept his recipes: Tyler Cowen's Ethnic Dining Guide still names it his default Fairfax pick (braised fish; bone-in Sichuan chili chicken). Open in 2026.

dish: hand-pulled laghman, dapanchi (big-plate chicken), lamb skewers, pilau, kathlama naan
w: Downtown Fairfax's window into Uyghur cooking — hand-pulled laghman 'thick and chewy, almost like udon,' the giant chicken-and-potato dapanchi, cumin-crusted lamb skewers and flaky kathlama naan. Named to Washingtonian's Cheap Eats and to Northern Virginia Magazine's 50 Best Restaurants, with a standalone NoVA Mag review. Halal; a genuine Central Asian rarity in the corridor.

dish: goat momos, poleko sekuwa (spiced skewers), timbur wings
w: A tiny 2026-opened family kitchen that Tyler Cowen's Ethnic Dining Guide immediately flagged as 'the real thing' — 'the goat momos are among the best dishes in northern Virginia right now,' most everything else at least very good. Unlike the region's Indian-leaning Nepali spots, it cooks true Nepali; FFXnow covered the couple's home-recipe opening. Small, fills up early.

dish: char kway teow, Hainanese chicken rice, nasi lemak, roti canai, Singaporean chili crab
w: A stylish Fairfax dining room (chefs from Malaysia and Singapore) that plates three Southeast Asian traditions honestly — the Washington Post's 2024 review, 'Three cuisines, one nice package,' singled out the char kway teow and Hainanese chicken rice, and Northern Virginia Magazine's First Bite praised the flaky roti canai. Halal. Cross-tagged Malaysian/Singaporean because the kitchen genuinely spans that hawker canon.

dish: chili crab with mantou, Hainanese chicken rice, seafood laksa, nasi lemak
w: The DC area's first fine-dining Singaporean restaurant, on the third floor of Tysons Galleria from chef Pepe Moncayo (of DC's Cranes) and his Singapore-born wife Aishah. The Washington Post's review called it 'a sublime taste of Singapore,' with the chili crab a stunner; Washingtonian, Arlington Magazine and DCist all covered the 2023 opening. 'Jiwa' means Singapore soul.

dish: cumin ribs, chili cabbage, minced pork with sour greens, Hunan specialties
w: The Vienna strip-mall Hunan kitchen (opened July 2025) that Washington Post critic Elazar Sontag gave three stars ('outstanding') and ranked No. 6 on his 2026 list of the 10 Best New Restaurants in the DC area — one of only two NoVA spots on it. Its deep menu of Hunan dishes 'you can't find in D.C.' set off a regional obsession, per FFXnow.

dish: somtum (five papaya salads), khao soi, whole fried rockfish, larb
address: 1307 Old Chain Bridge Rd, McLean, VA 22101
w: A snug McLean strip-mall room devoted to Northeastern (Isaan) Thai cooking — five versions of papaya salad, vividly spiced khao soi and a herb-and-cashew-smothered whole fried rockfish that draws the most praise. Named to Washingtonian's 100 Very Best Restaurants (#62) and reviewed in the Washington Post's $20 Diner; also covered by Arlington Magazine and Washington City Paper.

dish: goat curry, jhol momo, fulbari naan
w: The Nepali bistro that took over Vienna's shuttered Mo:Mo House on Maple Avenue, bringing goat curry, fulbari naan and a devoted momo following. Northern Virginia Magazine profiled its 'unique dishes' and Tysons Reporter covered its arrival — a well-liked Himalayan option on Vienna's restaurant row.

dish: Karachi-style paratha rolls, chicken tikka, chai
w: One of the four ambitious modern Pakistani spots Washingtonian spotlighted in 2024 — owner Suhail Kamran sent partners to Karachi to learn paratha rolls from a street vendor, and the parathas come out 'supple and pleasantly flaky.' Now expanded into a Tysons Corner Center cafe with a bigger drinks menu (FFXnow). A stylish, social-media-forward take on Pakistani street food.

dish: charcoal kabobs, kabuli palaw, mantu — fast-casual bowls
w: The Herndon fast-casual spinoff of the famed Helmand — the Afghan restaurant empire of the late Qayum Karzai (elder brother of Afghanistan's former president). Northern Virginia Magazine covered its arrival as 'Afghan food takes its turn in the fast-casual bowl world,' with the owners fierce about authentic Afghan cardamom and cinnamon over generic curry powders; Baltimore Magazine chronicles the Helmand lineage.

dish: chicken tikka kabobs, karahi, matka chai, falooda
w: A second-story Sterling Pakistani spot from Rawalpindi-born, Loudoun-raised Waqas Shah — Washingtonian's 2024 modern-Pakistani feature praised the charcoal kabobs, the bright-orange chicken tikka marinade permeating the meat, from a terrace with a runway view of Dulles landings. Fully halal and a bona fide DMV social-media favorite (viral on TikTok food creators). Street-food energy done ambitiously.
